title: Yoga in Panchang
subtitle: Understanding the twenty-seven Nitya Yogas formed from Sun and Moon longitudes
summary: This session introduces Yoga as one of the five limbs of Panchang. Students learn that Nitya Yoga is calculated from the sum of the sidereal longitudes of the Sun and Moon, that the full 360° cycle is divided into twenty-seven equal parts of 13°20′ each, how to calculate the running Yoga, and why Yoga should be read together with the other Panchang limbs rather than used alone.
learningObjectives: Define Nitya Yoga as a Panchang limb.
Explain how Sun and Moon longitudes are combined to calculate Yoga.
Name the twenty-seven Nitya Yogas in sequence.
Calculate the running Yoga from sidereal longitudes.
Normalise a longitude sum greater than 360°.
Distinguish Panchang Yoga from horoscope Yoga.
Understand the limits of using Yoga alone for judgement.
prerequisites: Completion of Session 6: Nakshatra and Pada.
Basic understanding of sidereal longitude, angular addition and normalising angles to 0°–360°.

keyTerms.meaning: One of twenty-seven daily Panchang Yogas calculated from the combined sidereal longitudes of the Sun and Moon.
The sum of the sidereal longitudes of the Sun and Moon.
keyTerms.note: If the sum is 360° or more, subtract 360°.

keyTerms.meaning: Bringing an angle into the standard 0°–360° range.
keyTerms.note: This is necessary before identifying the Yoga index.

keyTerms.meaning: The numbered position of the running Yoga from 1 to 27.
keyTerms.note: It is derived by dividing the normalised longitude sum by 13°20′.

keyTerms.meaning: A planetary combination in a birth chart formed through placement, lordship, conjunction or aspect.
keyTerms.note: This is different from the daily Nitya Yoga of Panchang.

blocks.text: Nitya Yoga is one of the five limbs of Panchang. It is determined by adding the sidereal longitudes of the Sun and Moon and locating the result within one of twenty-seven equal divisions of the zodiacal circle.

blocks.explanation: The complete longitude-sum cycle is divided into twenty-seven equal Yoga segments.
blocks.workedExample: A normalised sum from 0°00′ to less than 13°20′ belongs to Vishkambha, the first Yoga.

blocks.altText: A simple flow diagram showing Sun longitude and Moon longitude being added to produce the Panchang Yoga.
blocks.caption: Nitya Yoga is based on the sum of Sun and Moon sidereal longitudes.
blocks.purpose: Show the basic inputs and result of the Yoga calculation.

blocks.title: Yoga uses addition
blocks.text: Tithi uses the Moon–Sun difference, while Nitya Yoga uses the Sun–Moon sum.

blocks.caption: The twenty-seven Nitya Yogas in order
blocks.note: The sequence is fixed and repeats after Vaidhriti.

blocks.title: Names should be read with timing
blocks.text: A Yoga may end during the civil day, so its ending time is part of the Panchang entry.

blocks.expression: Raw sum = Sun sidereal longitude + Moon sidereal longitude
blocks.explanation: Both values must use the same sidereal zodiac and Ayanamsha.
blocks.workedExample: Sun 120° and Moon 210° give a raw sum of 330°.

blocks.explanation: If the raw sum is 360° or more, subtract 360° until it lies within 0°–360°.
blocks.workedExample: Sun 250° plus Moon 180° equals 430°. Normalised sum = 70°.

blocks.altText: A simple number-line style diagram showing a raw longitude sum above 360 degrees being reduced into the 0 to 360 degree range.
blocks.caption: The Sun–Moon longitude sum must be normalised before identifying the Yoga.
blocks.purpose: Explain why 360° is subtracted from large sums.

sections.title: How to Calculate the Running Yoga

blocks.workedExample: A normalised sum of 70° gives Yoga index 6, Atiganda.

blocks.title: Calculate a Yoga
blocks.scenario: Sun sidereal longitude is 100° and Moon sidereal longitude is 268°.

blocks.title: A second example
blocks.scenario: Sun sidereal longitude is 145° and Moon sidereal longitude is 100°.
steps: No normalisation is required because the sum is below 360°.
245° ÷ 13°20′ gives eighteen complete segments with remainder.

blocks.text: Each Yoga spans the same angular measure of 13°20′, but its clock duration is not fixed. The Sun and Moon move at changing apparent speeds, so their combined longitude reaches the next Yoga boundary at a variable time.

blocks.expression: Approximate Yoga duration = 13°20′ ÷ combined daily motion of Sun and Moon
blocks.explanation: A faster combined motion produces a shorter Yoga duration, while slower motion produces a longer duration.
blocks.workedExample: The exact duration must be calculated from ephemeris positions rather than assumed to be twenty-four hours.

blocks.title: Yoga can change during the day
blocks.text: Always read the Yoga ending time in a daily Panchang.

blocks.caption: Panchang Yoga and horoscope Yoga are different concepts.

blocks.title: Yoga is one supporting factor
blocks.text: A complete Panchang or Muhurta judgement should not be based on Nitya Yoga alone.

commonMistakes.mistake: Subtracting Sun longitude from Moon longitude to calculate Yoga.
commonMistakes.whyItIsWrong: That difference is used for Tithi, not Nitya Yoga.
commonMistakes.correctUnderstanding: Add Sun and Moon sidereal longitudes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to normalise a sum above 360°.
commonMistakes.whyItIsWrong: The Yoga index must be found within the 0°–360° cycle.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing Panchang Yoga with horoscope Yoga.
commonMistakes.whyItIsWrong: They are calculated through different rules and serve different purposes.
commonMistakes.correctUnderstanding: Nitya Yoga is a daily Panchang value; horoscope Yoga is a chart combination.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming Yoga lasts exactly twenty-four hours.
commonMistakes.whyItIsWrong: Its duration depends on changing Sun and Moon motion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using Yoga alone to declare an activity auspicious.
commonMistakes.whyItIsWrong: Yoga is only one of the five Panchang limbs.
commonMistakes.correctUnderstanding: Read it with Tithi, Vara, Nakshatra, Karana and the purpose of the activity.

sessionSummary: Nitya Yoga is one of the five limbs of Panchang.
It is calculated from the sum of Sun and Moon sidereal longitudes.
The longitude sum is normalised into the 0°–360° range.
The full cycle is divided into twenty-seven Yogas.
The Yoga index is calculated from the normalised sum.
Yoga duration varies because Sun and Moon motion varies.
The Yoga ending time is part of the daily Panchang entry.
Panchang Yoga is different from horoscope Yoga.
Nitya Yoga should not be used alone for complete judgement.

questions.question: Which operation is used to calculate Nitya Yoga?
questions.explanation: Nitya Yoga is calculated from the sum of the sidereal longitudes of the Sun and Moon.

questions.question: How many Nitya Yogas are there?
questions.explanation: The 360° longitude-sum cycle is divided into twenty-seven equal parts.

questions.question: What is the span of one Nitya Yoga?
What should be done if the Sun–Moon longitude sum is 430°?
questions.answer: Subtract 360° to obtain a normalised sum of 70°.
questions.explanation: Yoga calculation uses a normalised 0°–360° value.

questions.question: Panchang Yoga and horoscope Yoga are the same concept.
questions.explanation: Panchang Yoga is a daily longitude-sum value, while horoscope Yoga is a planetary combination.

questions.question: Which Yoga follows Siddhi?
questions.explanation: Siddhi is number 16 and Vyatipata is number 17.

questions.question: Every Nitya Yoga lasts exactly twenty-four hours.
questions.explanation: Its duration changes with the combined motion of the Sun and Moon.

questions.question: Why should Yoga not be used alone for complete Muhurta judgement?
questions.answer: Because it is only one Panchang limb and must be combined with Tithi, Vara, Nakshatra, Karana and other relevant factors.
